title: Design a data structure that supports adding words and searching words, where the search string may contain the dot character '.' that matches any single letter. Return whether any stored word matches the pattern.
shortTitle: Design Add and Search Words: Trie + DFS for '.' wildcard

s1_definition.oneliner: Build a Trie for insertion; search with DFS where a dot fans out to every child and a real character follows one exact child, succeeding when any path ends at a word marker.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Trie (prefix tree)** – a tree where each node holds child links for characters and an end-of-word flag; inserting a word walks or creates nodes character by character.
- **Wildcard dot** – the character `.` matches any single letter, so during search it branches into all children of the current node.
- **DFS search** – a recursive traversal that follows one child for a normal character and fans out to all children for a dot, returning true if any branch reaches an end-of-word at the pattern's end.
- **End-of-word check** – the base case when the pattern index reaches the end; the search succeeds only if the current node is marked as a word ending, not merely a prefix.
- **Branching cost** – with no dots, search is O(L) where L is the word length; each dot multiplies branching by the number of children at that level.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, support agents look up stored transaction references when a customer recites one imperfectly, typing a dot wherever they cannot recall a character. A known character takes one exact drawer in the reference directory, while a dot means try every drawer at that level. If one of the branching paths spells a complete stored reference, the lookup succeeds.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
         Trie Structure After Adding: loan, lore, loft

                    root
                     │
                   ┌─▼─┐
                   │ l │
                   └─┬─┘
                     │
                   ┌─▼─┐
                   │ o │
                   └─┬─┘
                ┌────┼────┐
              ┌─▼─┐┌─▼─┐┌─▼─┐
              │ a ││ r ││ f │
              └─┬─┘└─┬─┘└─┬─┘
              ┌─▼─┐┌─▼─┐┌─▼─┐
              │ n*││ e*││ t*│   * = end-of-word
              └───┘└───┘└───┘

         Search: lo.n

         Step 1: l -> follow exact child 'l'
         Step 2: o -> follow exact child 'o'
         Step 3: . -> fan out to ALL children: a, r, f
           Branch a: check 'n' in children of 'a' -> found, isEndOfWord=true => MATCH
           Branch r: check 'n' in children of 'r' -> not found => fail
           Branch f: check 'n' in children of 'f' -> not found => fail
         Result: true (one branch succeeded)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem extends a plain Trie with a search that understands the dot wildcard, which matches any single character. Adding a word is ordinary Trie insertion: walk the word from the root, create missing child nodes, and mark the final node as an end-of-word. The interesting part is the search.

Search is a recursive depth-first traversal parameterised by the current pattern index and the current node. When the pattern character is a normal letter, follow exactly one child link, failing if it does not exist. When the character is a dot, try every child of the current node and succeed if any recursive call succeeds, which is the fan-out that makes wildcards work. The base case is when the index reaches the end of the pattern, where the search returns whether the current node is marked as an end-of-word, not merely a prefix.

The cost with no dots is O(L) for a pattern of length L. Each dot multiplies branching by the number of children at that level, so a pattern of all dots could explore a large part of the Trie. In production, Rajesh limits the number of dots allowed or adds a timeout to protect the service.

At the National Bank of India, support agents used this to look up stored transaction references when a customer recited one imperfectly. The known characters pruned the search down one exact path, and only the unknown positions fanned out, so the lookup stayed focused on plausible references. The end-of-word check ensured that partial matches to longer references did not produce false positives.

Remember one sentence: insert words into a Trie normally, and search with DFS where a dot fans out to all children while a real character follows one, succeeding only when a branch reaches an end-of-word marker.

---

keyPoints: Insertion is standard Trie insertion: walk or create child nodes character by character and mark the final node as end-of-word.
Search is recursive DFS: a normal character follows one exact child, a dot fans out to all children of the current node.
The base case checks isEndOfWord, not just that the index reached the pattern end, to avoid matching mere prefixes.
With no dots, search is O(L) where L is the pattern length; each dot multiplies branching by the number of children at that level.
Iterate node.children.values() for dots rather than all 26 letters, because most nodes have few children.
This pattern is the foundation of regex engines, spell checkers, and autocomplete systems with partial-match support.
